presenterNotes: The Addition and Subtraction Properties of Inequality are straightforward extensions of the equation properties. The main new idea is graphing the solution set.
When the variable is on the right, remind students they can rewrite with the variable on the left by flipping the inequality symbol.
For the blueprint, stress that 'Understand' includes identifying the operation and the boundary, which sets up the solving step correctly.

formulaCard.formula: $$ a > b \;\Rightarrow\; a + c > b + c $$
formulaCard.title: Addition Property of Inequality
notes: Add the same number to both sides to isolate the variable.

rows.1: If $ a > b $, then $ a + c > b + c $
If $ a \ge b $, then $ a + c \ge b + c $

explanation: [[kw:Equivalent inequalities]] have the same solution set. We produce them using properties of inequality.
The [[kw:Addition Property of Inequality]]: Adding the same number to each side of an inequality produces an equivalent inequality.
If $ a > b $, then $ a + c > b + c $. This holds for all inequality symbols: >, <, ≥, ≤.
To solve an inequality like $ x - 6 \ge -10 $, add 6 to both sides to isolate the variable.
Always graph the solution on a number line, using a closed circle for ≥ or ≤, and shading the correct direction.

teacherCues: Write 'x - 6 ≥ -10' on the board and ask: 'What operation is being applied to x? How can we undo it?'
Display the number line for x ≥ -4. Ask: 'Why is -4 included, but -5 is not?'

steps: Add 6 to both sides: $ x - 6 + 6 \ge -10 + 6 $.
Simplify: $ x \ge -4 $.
Graph: closed circle at -4, shade right. Check: $ x = 0 $ gives $ 0 - 6 \ge -10 $ → $ -6 \ge -10 $ ✓
examples.title: A – Solving by Adding

examples.peerPrompt: Explain to a partner: Why does adding 2 to both sides give the solution, and why is the circle open?
steps: Add 2 to both sides: $ b > -7 $.
Graph: open circle at -7, shade right.

C – Variable on the Right
steps: Add $ \frac{1}{4} $ to both sides: $ \frac{1}{4} + \frac{1}{4} > y $ → $ \frac{1}{2} > y $.
Rewrite as $ y < \frac{1}{2} $. Graph: open circle at 0.5, shade left.

blocks.title: Addition Property of Inequality

confusionCorner.title: Which Side to Add?
confusionCorner.body: In $ \frac{1}{4} > y - \frac{1}{4} $, the variable is on the right. You still add $ \frac{1}{4} $ to both sides. After simplifying, you may rewrite as $ y < \frac{1}{2} $ to have the variable on the left. [[imp:If you swap sides, flip the inequality symbol.]]

discoveryHook.scenario: Just like equations, inequalities stay balanced when you add the same number to both sides. If you have a few dollars less than your friend, giving both of you $5 keeps the same relationship – you're still behind, but the gap doesn't change. The Addition Property of Inequality keeps that balance intact!

blocks.title: Subtraction Property of Inequality

confusionCorner.body: An answer like $ -9.4 < m $ is correct, but standard form is $ m > -9.4 $. When you flip the order, you must [[imp:flip the inequality symbol]] so the small end still points to the smaller value.
confusionCorner.title: Rewriting with Variable on the Left

discoveryHook.scenario: Subtracting the same number from both sides of an inequality is just as fair as adding. If you're heavier than your sibling by a few pounds, and you both lose the same weight, you'll still be heavier – the inequality remains. That's the Subtraction Property of Inequality in action!

hints: The operation on k is addition.

Solve $ p + 0.7 > -2.3 $. What is the solution inequality?

hints: The circle is placed at the boundary.

teacherCues: Write 'y + 8 ≤ 5' and ask: 'How is this different from the previous examples? What operation will undo the +8?'
Display -8 < 1.4 + m and guide students to rewrite it as m + 1.4 > -8 before solving.

explanation: The [[kw:Subtraction Property of Inequality]]: Subtracting the same number from each side produces an equivalent inequality.
If $ a > b $, then $ a - c > b - c $. This holds for all inequality symbols.
To solve $ y + 8 \le 5 $, subtract 8 from both sides.
When the variable is on the right, like $ -8 < 1.4 + m $, subtract 1.4 and then rewrite with the variable on the left, flipping the symbol.

rows.1: If $ a > b $, then $ a - c > b - c $
If $ a \ge b $, then $ a - c \ge b - c $

formulaCard.formula: $$ a > b \;\Rightarrow\; a - c > b - c $$
notes: Subtract the same number from both sides.
Works the same as the Addition Property.
formulaCard.title: Subtraction Property of Inequality

examples.title: A – Solving by Subtracting
steps: Subtract 8 from both sides: $ y \le -3 $.
Graph: closed circle at -3, shade left.
Check: $ y = -4 $ gives $ -4 + 8 \le 5 $ → $ 4 \le 5 $ ✓
Subtract 1.4 from both sides: $ -9.4 < m $.
Rewrite: $ m > -9.4 $.
Graph: open circle at -9.4, shade right.
examples.title: B – Variable on the Right
examples.peerPrompt: Explain to a partner: After solving, how do we rewrite $ -9.4 < m $ as $ m > -9.4 $, and why is the graph an open circle?

steps: Subtract $ \frac{1}{6} $ from both sides: $ \frac{4}{6} \le z $.
Rewrite: $ z \ge \frac{2}{3} $. Graph: closed circle at 2/3, shade right.

explanation: If one or both sides of an inequality can be simplified, do that first.
[[imp:Combine like terms]] on each side, just as you did with equations.
Then use the Addition or Subtraction Property to isolate the variable.
This makes the inequality look simpler and reduces mistakes.

notes: Combine like terms on the left and/or right first.
Then apply the Addition or Subtraction Property of Inequality.
formulaCard.title: Simplify, Then Use Properties

Graph: open circle at 2, shade left.
examples.title: A – Combine Constants
B – Combine Variable Terms
steps: Combine $ 3p - 2p = p $: $ 10 \ge p - 7 $.
Add 7 to both sides: $ 17 \ge p $, or $ p \le 17 $.
Graph: closed circle at 17, shade left.
examples.peerPrompt: Explain to a partner: Why did we combine 3p and -2p before moving the constant?

examples.title: C – Simplify Both Sides
steps: Left: $ 18 + z $. Right: 9. Inequality: $ 18 + z > 9 $.
Subtract 18: $ z > -9 $.
Graph: open circle at -9, shade right.

confusionCorner.title: Only Combine on the Same Side
confusionCorner.body: You cannot combine terms across the inequality symbol. In $ 10 \ge 3p - 2p - 7 $, combine $ 3p $ and $ -2p $ on the right only. The 10 on the left stays separate until you move it.

discoveryHook.scenario: Sometimes an inequality has extra numbers hanging around the variable. Just like cleaning up your desk before starting homework, combine like terms first. A tidy inequality is easier to solve and graph!

blocks.title: Simplifying Before Solving

formulaCard.title: Writing an Inequality from Words
notes: Symbol depends on phrase: 'at most' → ≤, 'more than' → >, etc.
Solve by subtracting the current amount from both sides.

explanation: Real‑world problems often involve an unknown amount that you can add or subtract while staying under (or over) a limit.
Write a verbal model, then translate into an inequality.
Use the Addition or Subtraction Property to solve.
Interpret the solution in the context: if $ w < 700 $, you can add any amount less than 700 watts.

discoveryHook.scenario: From packing a bag for a flight (weight limit 50 pounds) to plugging in appliances without blowing a fuse, inequalities help you stay within safe limits. You don't need the exact number – you just need to know how much more you can add before hitting the ceiling!

confusionCorner.body: In the circuit example, the maximum is 1800 W, and going over blows a fuse. So we use <, not ≤. In the bag example, 'no more than 50 pounds' includes exactly 50, so we use ≤. [[imp:Pay attention to whether the boundary is allowed.]]
confusionCorner.title: Strict vs. Non‑Strict

examples.title: A – Circuit Overload
steps: Verbal model: 1100 + w < 1800.
Subtract 1100: $ w < 700 $.
You can add any amount less than 700 watts.
examples.prompt: A microwave uses 1100 W. The circuit overloads at 1800 W. Write and solve an inequality for additional watts w you can add.
A carry‑on bag weighs 38 lb, max 50 lb. Write and solve an inequality for how much weight x you can add.

steps: 'No more than 50 pounds' means ≤ 50.
Inequality: $ 38 + x \le 50 $.
Subtract 38: $ x \le 12 $. You can add up to 12 lb.

explanation: The [[imp:Understand → Solve → Conclude]] blueprint applies to inequalities as well.
